A.explanation: A triangular $a$-$t$ graph would mean acceleration changes steadily, which would make the $s$-$t$ graph curved, not straight lines.

B.explanation: A non-zero constant $a$ would mean velocity changes steadily, but the $s$-$t$ slopes are constant so velocity is constant on each straight section.

C.explanation: Constant positive then negative $a$ would give a parabolic $s$-$t$ shape, not the straight-line up and down sections shown.

D.explanation: Straight $s$-$t$ sections have constant velocity so $a = 0$, with only brief large spikes where velocity reverses sharply at the peaks and troughs.

hints: Notice the $s$-$t$ graph is made of straight line segments with constant positive slope then constant negative slope.
Recall that the gradient of $s$-$t$ is velocity $v$ and the gradient of $v$-$t$ is acceleration $a$, so constant $v$ means $a = 0$.
Think about what must happen to $v$ at the sharp peaks where motion instantly changes from moving away to moving back, and which $a$-$t$ graph shows zero almost everywhere with spikes there.
walkthrough: The $s$-$t$ graph shows two identical triangles: $s$ increases linearly with $t$, then decreases linearly back to zero, then repeats.

Velocity is the gradient of displacement, $v = \Delta s / \Delta t$. A straight $s$-$t$ line has constant gradient, so $v$ is a positive constant on the rising part and a negative constant on the falling part.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$. While $v$ is constant, $\Delta v = 0$ so $a = 0$ for almost all the time.

At each sharp peak and each point where $s$ returns to zero, $v$ changes almost instantly from one constant value to the opposite value, so $a$ is briefly very large in the negative or positive sense.
Therefore the $a$-$t$ graph is zero everywhere except for short spikes at the turning times. This is option D.
